lessons.title: Floor of Fourth Ventricle
quickRevision: Diamond-shaped (rhomboid) fossa formed by posterior surface of pons (upper half) and open medulla (lower half).
Divided into right & left halves by median sulcus; horizontal striae medullares separate pontine and medullary parts.
Medial eminence shows facial colliculus (abducens nucleus + internal genu of facial nerve) in pons, and hypoglossal & vagal triangles in medulla.
Inferior angle has obex and area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone / vomiting center).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Introduction & Shape (rhomboid fossa) → 2. Boundaries (superolateral & inferolateral) → 3. Divisions (pontine, intermediate/striae medullares, medullary) → 4. Features in Pontine Part (facial colliculus, locus coeruleus) → 5. Features in Medullary Part (hypoglossal triangle, vagal triangle, vestibular area, calamus scriptorius, area postrema) → 6. Neat labelled diagram (compulsory!).

slides.h: 1. What is it & Where is it located?
slides.p: The floor of the fourth ventricle is also called the rhomboid fossa because it is shaped like a diamond (rhombus). It lies on the back (posterior surface) of the brainstem—specifically, its upper triangular half is formed by the posterior surface of the pons, and its lower triangular half is formed by the posterior surface of the open part of the medulla oblongata.
bullets: Superolateral boundaries: Superior cerebellar peduncles (on each side).
Inferolateral boundaries: Gracile tubercle, cuneate tubercle, and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Median sulcus: Runs vertically down the center, dividing the floor into symmetrical right and left halves.
slides.remember: Diamond floor = Upper half Pons + Lower half Open Medulla, split vertically by the Median Sulcus.
slides.q: Which two parts of the brainstem form the floor of the fourth ventricle?
opts: Posterior pons and open medulla oblongata
slides.why: The upper triangular half is formed by the posterior pons, and the lower triangular half is formed by the posterior surface of the open medulla.

slides.h: 2. Important Structures in the Pontine (Upper) Part
slides.p: Lateral to the median sulcus lies a vertical elevation called the medial eminence, bounded laterally by the sulcus limitans. In the pontine region, the lower end of the medial eminence swells to form the facial colliculus. At the upper end of the sulcus limitans is a bluish-grey area called the locus coeruleus (rich in noradrenergic neurons).
bullets: Facial colliculus: Produced by motor fibres of the facial nerve (CN VII) looping around the abducens nucleus (CN VI).
Striae medullares: Delicate white transverse fibres crossing the middle of the floor from lateral recesses to the median sulcus, marking the junction between pontine and medullary parts.
Vestibular area: Lies lateral to the sulcus limitans across both pontine and medullary parts.
slides.remember: Facial colliculus = CN VII fibres looping over CN VI nucleus (NOT the facial nucleus itself!).
slides.q: The facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by fibres of the facial nerve looping around which nucleus?
slides.why: The motor fibres of the facial nerve (CN VII) wind around the abducens nucleus (CN VI) internally, producing the surface bump called the facial colliculus.

slides.p: The lower tapered tip of the floor resembles the nib of a writing pen and is called the calamus scriptorius. In this medullary triangle, the sulcus limitans splits into two small depressions that outline three key triangles: the hypoglossal triangle (medially), the vagal triangle (between them), and the vestibular area (laterally). Just above the inferior angle (obex) lies the area postrema.
bullets: Hypoglossal triangle: Overlies the hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII).
Vagal triangle: Overlies the dorsal nucleus of vagus (CN X).

Clinical — Area Postrema: Lacks a blood-brain barrier and acts as the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) for vomiting. Tumors in the 4th ventricle (like medulloblastoma or ependymoma) cause projectile vomiting and obstructive hydrocephalus.
slides.remember: From medial to lateral in lower floor: Hypoglossal (XII) → Vagal (X) → Vestibular (VIII). Tip = Calamus scriptorius + Area postrema (vomiting).
slides.q: Which structure at the inferior angle of the fourth ventricle acts as the chemoreceptor trigger zone (vomiting center)?
slides.why: The area postrema lies just rostral to the obex in the floor of the fourth ventricle and serves as the chemoreceptor trigger zone for emesis.

lessons.title: Corpus Callosum
quickRevision: Largest commissural fibre bundle (~10 cm long, >200 million axons) connecting matching areas of left & right cerebral hemispheres.
4 parts from anterior to posterior: Rostrum → Genu → Trunk (Body) → Splenium.
Genu forms Forceps Minor (frontal lobes); Splenium forms Forceps Major (occipital lobes) and Tapetum.
Blood supply: Pericallosal artery (branch of Anterior Cerebral Artery); Splenium also gets Posterior Cerebral Artery supply.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Fibre Type (largest commissural bundle) → 2. Location & Dimensions (floor of median longitudinal fissure, 10 cm) → 3. Four Parts & Relations (Rostrum, Genu, Trunk, Splenium) → 4. Fibre Projections (Forceps minor, Forceps major, Tapetum) → 5. Blood Supply → 6. Clinical Anatomy (Split-brain syndrome, Marchiafava-Bignami disease) + Sagittal/Horizontal diagram.

slides.h: 1. What is it, Location & Four Parts?
slides.p: The corpus callosum is the largest bundle of commissural fibres in the brain. Commissural fibres connect corresponding (homotopic) areas of the left and right cerebral hemispheres so both sides of your brain can talk to each other. It lies at the bottom of the median longitudinal fissure and forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
bullets: Rostrum: Thin, beak-like anterior-inferior prolongation extending back to the lamina terminalis.
Genu: Anterior bent end ('knee'), lying ~4 cm behind the frontal pole.
Trunk (Body): Main arched middle portion extending backward; superior surface is covered by indusium griseum and cingulate gyrus.
Splenium: Thickest, rounded posterior end lying ~6 cm in front of the occipital pole, overhanging the pineal gland and midbrain tectum.
slides.remember: R-G-T-S from front to back: Rostrum (beak) → Genu (knee) → Trunk (body) → Splenium (thick tail).
slides.q: Which is the thickest and most posterior part of the corpus callosum?
slides.why: The splenium is the thickest, rounded posterior extremity of the corpus callosum, overhanging the pineal body and dorsal midbrain.

slides.p: As the fibres of the corpus callosum fan out into the white matter of both hemispheres, they form named bundles that are classic viva and MCQ favorites:
bullets: Forceps Minor: Fibres from the genu curve forward like a fork to connect both frontal lobes.
Forceps Major: Fibres from the splenium curve backward to connect both occipital lobes (producing the bulb of the posterior horn).
Tapetum: Fibres from the posterior trunk and splenium sweep downward to form the roof and lateral wall of the posterior and inferior horns of the lateral ventricle.
Blood Supply: Mainly by the pericallosal artery (branch of Anterior Cerebral Artery). The splenium is additionally supplied by posterior pericallosal branches of the Posterior Cerebral Artery.
slides.remember: Genu = Forceps Minor (Frontal). Splenium = Forceps Major (Occipital) + Tapetum.
slides.q: Which bundle of callosal fibres curves backward from the splenium to connect the two occipital lobes?
slides.why: Forceps major consists of fibres passing through the splenium that curve posteriorly into the occipital lobes.

slides.p: Understanding what happens when the corpus callosum is cut or damaged helps you score extra clinical marks in your short note:
bullets: Callosotomy (Split-Brain Syndrome): Surgical sectioning of the corpus callosum is sometimes performed to control intractable generalized epilepsy. Patients cannot transfer learned information between hemispheres (e.g., an object held in the left hand—processed by the right hemisphere—cannot be named verbally because speech is in the left hemisphere).
Agenesis of Corpus Callosum: Congenital absence of the corpus callosum; MRI shows widely separated parallel lateral ventricles ('racing car sign').
Marchiafava-Bignami Disease: Rare demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum associated with chronic alcoholism.
slides.remember: Split-brain = Left hand feels object (Right brain), Right brain can't tell Left brain (speech) what it is!
slides.q: Which artery is the primary blood supply to the rostrum, genu, and trunk of the corpus callosum?
opts: Pericallosal artery (branch of Anterior Cerebral Artery)
slides.why: The pericallosal artery, a continuation of the anterior cerebral artery, runs directly above the corpus callosum and supplies its rostrum, genu, and body.

lessons.title: Internal Capsule
quickRevision: Compact V-shaped band of projection fibres between thalamus/caudate medially and lentiform nucleus laterally.
5 parts: Anterior limb, Genu, Posterior limb, Retrolentiform part, Sublentiform part.
Genu carries Corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibres; Posterior limb carries Corticospinal tract + Superior thalamic radiation.
Blood supply: Charcot's artery of cerebral hemorrhage (lateral striate branch of MCA) supplies posterior limb → thrombosis causes contralateral hemiplegia.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Fibre Type (projection fibres) → 2. Relations (medial & lateral in horizontal section) → 3. Five Parts & Exact Fibre Composition (table format shines!) → 4. Blood Supply (artery-by-artery for each part) → 5. Applied Anatomy (capsular hemiplegia, Charcot's artery) + Horizontal section diagram.

slides.h: 1. What is it & Relations in Horizontal Section?
slides.p: The internal capsule is a thick, compact V-shaped sheet of projection fibres (ascending sensory and descending motor tracts) connecting the cerebral cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord. Because so many vital fibres are packed into a narrow space, even a tiny stroke here causes widespread paralysis.
bullets: Medial relations: Head of the caudate nucleus (anteriorly) and the thalamus (posteriorly).
Lateral relation: The lens-shaped lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus + putamen), which fits into the lateral concavity of the 'V'.
Continuity: Above, it fans out as the corona radiata; below, its motor fibres continue into the midbrain as the crus cerebri.
slides.remember: Think of a V-shaped highway: Caudate & Thalamus on the inside (medial), Lentiform nucleus on the outside (lateral).
slides.q: Which structures form the medial relations of the internal capsule in a horizontal section of the cerebrum?
opts: Head of caudate nucleus and thalamus
slides.why: Medially, the internal capsule is bounded by the head of the caudate nucleus in front and the dorsal thalamus behind.

slides.p: The internal capsule is divided into five parts based on their relation to the lentiform nucleus. Memorizing which tract runs in each part is the core of any LAQ or viva:
bullets: 1. Anterior Limb (between caudate head & lentiform): Frontopontine fibres and Anterior thalamic radiation.
2. Genu (bend of the V): Corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibres for head & neck muscles + Superior thalamic radiation.
3. Posterior Limb (between thalamus & lentiform): Corticospinal tract (upper limb in front, trunk, lower limb behind), Corticorubral fibres, and Superior thalamic radiation (somatosensory).
4. Retrolentiform Part (behind lentiform): Optic radiation (geniculocalcarine tract) and Parieto-/Occipitopontine fibres.
5. Sublentiform Part (below lentiform): Auditory radiation (from medial geniculate body to auditory cortex) and Temporopontine fibres.
slides.remember: Genu = Head/Neck (Corticonuclear). Posterior limb = Body motor (Corticospinal) + Sensory. Retro = Vision (Optic). Sub = Hearing (Auditory).
slides.q: Which part of the internal capsule contains the auditory radiation?
slides.why: The sublentiform part passes beneath the lentiform nucleus and carries the auditory radiation from the medial geniculate body to the temporal cortex.

slides.p: The internal capsule has a rich but vulnerable arterial supply from branches of the ICA, ACA, and MCA. Damage here produces classic upper motor neuron (UMN) syndromes:
bullets: Anterior limb: Recurrent artery of Heubner (branch of ACA) + medial/lateral striate branches of MCA.
Genu: Direct branches from Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) and lateral striate branches of MCA.
Posterior limb: Lateral striate branches of MCA (especially Charcot's artery of cerebral hemorrhage) and Anterior choroidal artery.
Retrolentiform & Sublentiform parts: Anterior choroidal artery (branch of ICA).

Clinical — Capsular Hemiplegia: Hemorrhage or thrombosis of Charcot's artery damages the posterior limb, causing contralateral spastic hemiplegia (paralysis of opposite half of body), contralateral hemianesthesia, and contralateral homonymous hemianopia (if retrolentiform fibres are involved).
slides.remember: Charcot's artery (branch of MCA) supplies the Posterior Limb → Stroke causes Contralateral Hemiplegia.
slides.q: Charcot's artery of cerebral hemorrhage is a branch of which major cerebral artery?
slides.why: Charcot's artery is the largest lateral lenticulostriate branch of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), frequently involved in hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.

lessons.title: Circle of Willis
quickRevision: Hexagonal arterial anastomosis in the interpeduncular cistern at the base of the brain.
Formed by 2 arterial systems: Internal Carotid (anterior) + Vertebrobasilar (posterior).
Branches: Cortical branches (ACA, MCA, PCA) and Central/Perforating branches (supply internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus).
Clinical: Berry aneurysms occur most commonly at arterial junctions (especially ACom–ACA junction) → Subarachnoid hemorrhage.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Location (interpeduncular fossa) → 2. Formation (Anterior, Lateral, Posterior boundaries—list exact arteries) → 3. Functional Significance (equalizes pressure, collateral flow) → 4. Types of Branches (Cortical vs Central) → 5. Applied Anatomy (Berry aneurysm, Subarachnoid hemorrhage) + Neat hexagonal diagram.

slides.h: 1. What is it & How is it Formed?
slides.p: The Circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus) is a polygonal (six-sided) arterial ring located at the base of the brain in the interpeduncular cistern, surrounding the optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, and mammillary bodies. It unites the anterior (internal carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations.
bullets: Anteriorly: Two Anterior Cerebral Arteries (ACA) joined together by the single Anterior Communicating Artery (ACom).
Anterolaterally (on each side): Terminal part of the Internal Carotid Artery (ICA).
Posterolaterally (on each side): Posterior Communicating Artery (PCom) connecting ICA to PCA.
Posteriorly: Bifurcation of the Basilar Artery into right and left Posterior Cerebral Arteries (PCA).
slides.remember: Note a classic trick: The Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) is a branch of ICA, NOT part of the ring itself!
slides.q: Which of the following arteries does NOT form part of the arterial ring of the Circle of Willis?
slides.why: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) arises from the internal carotid artery and runs laterally into the lateral sulcus; it is a major branch, not one of the arteries forming the polygon.

slides.p: Why did nature design a ring of arteries at the base of the brain? Under normal conditions, blood from the right and left sides barely mixes because pressures are equal. However, if one main feeding artery (like one ICA) gets slowly narrowed or blocked, the Circle of Willis provides a collateral pathway so blood from the opposite side can perfuse the deprived brain region.
bullets: Cortical branches: ACA, MCA, and PCA supply the cerebral cortex and have limited anastomoses on the brain surface.

Central (perforating) branches: Slender end-arteries arising directly from the circle (e.g., medial & lateral striate, thalamoperforating) that pierce the anterior and posterior perforated substances to supply deep structures (internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus).
slides.remember: Cortical branches = surface of brain. Central branches = functional end-arteries to deep grey matter & internal capsule.
slides.q: What is the primary physiological role of the Circle of Willis?
opts: Draining venous blood into the cavernous sinus
Providing collateral blood flow and equalizing arterial pressure between hemispheres
Secreting cerebrospinal fluid into the third ventricle
Supplying blood to the spinal cord
slides.why: The Circle of Willis equalizes blood pressure on both sides and acts as an emergency collateral bypass if one major feeding vessel is occluded.

slides.p: At the sharp Y-junctions where arteries of the Circle of Willis meet, the tunica media (muscular wall) can have congenital weak spots. Over time, high arterial pressure causes balloon-like outpouchings called saccular (berry) aneurysms.
bullets: Most common site: Junction of the Anterior Communicating Artery (ACom) and Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) (~30–35%), followed by the ICA–PCom junction.
Rupture consequence: Causes sudden, severe subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), classically described by patients as the 'worst headache of my life' (thunderclap headache) with neck stiffness.
PCom aneurysm sign: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm sits right next to the oculomotor nerve (CN III) and can compress it, causing ptosis, 'down-and-out' eye, and a dilated fixed pupil.
slides.remember: Berry aneurysm = Weak tunica media at junctions (ACom-ACA #1) → Rupture causes Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
slides.q: Where do congenital saccular (berry) aneurysms occur most frequently in the Circle of Willis?
opts: Junction of basilar and vertebral arteries
Junction of anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries
slides.why: The junction of the anterior communicating artery (ACom) with the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) is the single most common site for berry aneurysms.

lessons.title: Medial Medullary Syndrome
quickRevision: Also called Dejerine's Anterior Bulbar Syndrome.
Caused by occlusion of paramedian branches of Anterior Spinal Artery (or vertebral artery).

3 key structures damaged: 1. Pyramid (corticospinal) → Contralateral hemiplegia; 2. Medial lemniscus → Contralateral loss of vibration & proprioception; 3. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) → Ipsilateral tongue paralysis & deviation toward lesion.
Classic 'Alternating Hemiplegia': Contralateral body paralysis + Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Synonym (Dejerine syndrome) → 2. Artery Involved (paramedian branches of Anterior Spinal Artery) → 3. Structures Damaged & Clinical Deficit Table (3 structures = 3 deficits!) → 4. Why Tongue Deviates to Same Side (genioglossus action) → 5. T.S. Medulla diagram shading the medial wedge.

slides.h: 1. What is it & Which Artery is Blocked?
slides.p: Medial medullary syndrome (also known as Dejerine's syndrome) is a classic brainstem stroke syndrome caused by thrombosis or occlusion of the paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery (or directly from the vertebral artery). These branches supply the medial wedge of the medulla oblongata right next to the midline.
bullets: Zone affected: Paramedian (anteromedial) zone of the open medulla.

Core clinical pattern: It produces crossed (alternating) hemiplegia—meaning motor/sensory loss on the opposite (contralateral) side of the body, combined with a cranial nerve palsy on the same (ipsilateral) side.
slides.remember: Medial Medulla = M for Medial, M for Motor (Pyramid), M for Medial Lemniscus, and CN XII (12) divides evenly into Medial!
slides.q: Occlusion of which artery causes Medial Medullary Syndrome?
opts: Paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery
slides.why: Medial medullary syndrome results from occlusion of the paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery (or vertebral artery).

slides.h: 2. The Three Structures Damaged & Their Clinical Features
slides.p: Think of a neat triangle right next to the midline of the medulla. Three vital structures sit inside this paramedian territory, giving three unmistakable clinical signs:
bullets: 1. Pyramid (Corticospinal tract): Fibres have NOT crossed yet (they decussate lower down in the closed medulla). Result → Contralateral spastic hemiplegia (paralysis of arm and leg on the opposite side, sparing the face).
2. Medial Lemniscus: Fibres HAVE already crossed (internal arcuate fibres). Result → Contralateral loss of proprioception (position sense), vibration, and discriminative touch.

3. Hypoglossal Nerve Fibres (CN XII): Lower motor neuron fibres exiting between pyramid and olive. Result → Ipsilateral paralysis and atrophy of tongue muscles; on protrusion, the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed (lesion) side.
slides.remember: 3 structures in the wedge: Pyramid (opposite body weak) + Medial Lemniscus (opposite vibration/joint sense lost) + CN XII (same-side tongue weakness).
slides.q: In a patient with right-sided medial medullary syndrome, which way does the tongue deviate when protruded?
slides.why: Lower motor neuron damage to the right hypoglossal nerve paralyzes the right genioglossus; the unopposed left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the right (lesion) side.

slides.h: 3. Quick Comparison: Medial vs Lateral Medullary Syndrome
slides.p: Examiners love asking how to distinguish Medial Medullary Syndrome from Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome in viva and MCQs:
bullets: Artery: Medial = Anterior spinal artery; Lateral = PICA (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery) or vertebral artery.
Limb weakness: Present in Medial (pyramid damaged); ABSENT in Lateral (pyramid spared).
Dysphagia & Hoarseness: Absent in Medial; Present in Lateral (nucleus ambiguus — CN IX, X damaged).
Tongue paralysis: Present in Medial (CN XII); Absent in Lateral.
slides.remember: Rule of 4s: Midline nuclei are factors of 12 (3, 4, 6, 12). CN 12 is midline → Medial Medullary Syndrome!
slides.q: Which of the following is a classic feature of Medial Medullary Syndrome?
opts: Loss of pain and temperature on the contralateral body
Contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception
Dysphagia and loss of gag reflex
slides.why: Damage to the medial lemniscus causes contralateral loss of dorsal-column sensations (proprioception, vibration, and fine touch). Pain/temperature, Horner's, and dysphagia belong to Lateral Medullary Syndrome.

lessons.title: Brown-Séquard Syndrome
quickRevision: Caused by hemisection (cutting one lateral half) of the spinal cord (e.g., stab injury, tumor compression).
At the level of lesion (Ipsilateral): LMN paralysis (anterior horn) + complete loss of all sensations (posterior horn/root).
Below the level of lesion (Ipsilateral): UMN spastic paralysis (lateral corticospinal tract) + loss of vibration & proprioception (dorsal columns).
Below the level of lesion (Contralateral): Loss of pain & temperature starting 1–2 segments below (lateral spinothalamic tract already crossed!).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Etiology (hemisection of spinal cord) → 2. Anatomical Principle (decussation levels of the 3 major tracts) → 3. Clinical Features AT the Level of Lesion → 4. Clinical Features BELOW the Level (Ipsilateral vs Contralateral table) → 5. Diagram showing spinal cord tracts & crossing levels.

slides.h: 1. What is it & The Golden Rule of Tract Crossing?
slides.p: Brown-Séquard syndrome is the clinical picture produced by hemisection (damage to one lateral half, left or right) of the spinal cord, most commonly due to penetrating trauma (stab/gunshot) or extramedullary spinal tumors. You don't need to memorize the symptoms blindly—just look at where each tract crosses the midline!
bullets: 1. Lateral Corticospinal Tract (Motor): Already crossed in the medulla → descends on the same side.
2. Dorsal Columns — Fasciculus Gracilis & Cuneatus (Proprioception & Vibration): Ascend on the same side and cross higher up in the medulla.
3. Lateral Spinothalamic Tract (Pain & Temperature): Enters spinal cord, ascends 1–2 segments in Lissauer's tract, and crosses immediately to the opposite side via the anterior white commissure!
slides.remember: Motor & Dorsal Columns cross in the MEDULLA (same side in cord). Pain/Temp crosses in the SPINAL CORD (opposite side!).
slides.q: Why is pain and temperature lost on the contralateral (opposite) side below the lesion in Brown-Séquard syndrome?
opts: Because the lateral spinothalamic tract crosses in the medulla
Because spinothalamic fibres decussate within the spinal cord 1–2 segments above entry
Because the dorsal columns carry pain fibres
Because anterior horn cells cross over
slides.why: Second-order neurons of the lateral spinothalamic tract decussate within the spinal cord (1–2 segments above entry), so a right hemisection interrupts pain/temperature fibres coming from the left side of the body.

slides.h: 2. Clinical Features BELOW the Level of Lesion
slides.p: Suppose a patient has a right-sided hemisection at T10. Below T10, the findings split neatly into ipsilateral (right) and contralateral (left):
bullets: Ipsilateral (Same Side) UMN Paralysis: Damage to lateral corticospinal tract causes spastic paralysis, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and positive Babinski sign below the lesion.
Ipsilateral (Same Side) Loss of Proprioception & Vibration: Damage to dorsal columns causes loss of joint position sense, vibration, and two-point discrimination.
Contralateral (Opposite Side) Loss of Pain & Temperature: Damage to the already-crossed lateral spinothalamic tract causes analgesia and thermoanesthesia starting 1–2 segments below the lesion level.
slides.remember: Same side = Spastic weakness + Vibration/Position gone. Opposite side = Pain/Temperature gone (1–2 segments below).
slides.q: In a left-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T8, where will the patient lose vibration and joint position sense?
slides.why: Dorsal column fibres ascend ipsilaterally in the spinal cord before crossing in the medulla, so a left cord hemisection causes ipsilateral (left-sided) loss of vibration and proprioception below T8.

slides.h: 3. Clinical Features AT the Level of Lesion
slides.p: Don't forget what happens right at the exact segment that is sliced! At the level of the hemisection, entering dorsal roots and local anterior horn cells on that single segment are destroyed:
bullets: Ipsilateral Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Paralysis: Destruction of anterior horn cells at that segment causes flaccid paralysis, muscle wasting, and loss of reflexes in the muscles supplied by that specific segment.

Ipsilateral Band of Complete Anesthesia: Destruction of entering dorsal root fibres causes total loss of ALL sensations (pain, temperature, touch, proprioception) in a narrow dermatome band on the same side at the lesion level.
slides.remember: AT the lesion (same side) = LMN flaccid band + Total sensory loss band in that exact dermatome.
slides.q: At the exact segmental level of a spinal cord hemisection, what type of motor paralysis occurs on the ipsilateral side?
opts: No motor paralysis occurs at the level of lesion
slides.why: Direct destruction of anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) at the level of the lesion produces ipsilateral segmental LMN (flaccid) paralysis.

lessons.title: T.S. Midbrain – Superior Colliculus Level
quickRevision: Divided into 3 parts from posterior to anterior: Tectum (superior colliculi), Tegmentum, and Basis Pedunculi (Crus cerebri + Substantia nigra).
Key grey matter: Superior colliculus, Pretectal nucleus (pupillary light reflex), Oculomotor nuclear complex (CN III) + Edinger-Westphal nucleus, Red nucleus, Substantia nigra.
Tracts in Crus Cerebri (medial to lateral): Frontopontine (1/6) → Pyramidal tracts (middle 2/3) → Temporopontine/Parietopontine (1/6).
Clinical: Weber's syndrome (crus cerebri + CN III) and Benedikt's syndrome (red nucleus + medial lemniscus + CN III).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Gross Divisions (Tectum, Cerebral Aqueduct, Tegmentum, Substantia Nigra, Crus Cerebri) → 2. Grey Matter Nuclei (Superior colliculus, Pretectal, CN III + Edinger-Westphal, Red nucleus, Substantia nigra) → 3. White Matter Tracts (Crus cerebri proportions, Lemniscus, MLF, Rubrospinal decussation) → 4. Clinical Anatomy (Weber's & Benedikt's syndromes) + Transverse section diagram.

slides.p: A transverse section of the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus shows the narrow cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) surrounded by periaqueductal grey matter. Behind the aqueduct is the tectum; in front of it are the right and left cerebral peduncles, each split by the pigmented substantia nigra into an anterior crus cerebri and a posterior tegmentum.
bullets: Superior Colliculus: Layered grey-and-white structure controlling visual reflexes and saccadic eye movements; connected to lateral geniculate body via superior brachium.
Pretectal Nucleus: Lies just rostral/lateral to superior colliculus; mediates the pupillary light reflex.
Oculomotor Nucleus (CN III) & Edinger-Westphal Nucleus: Situated in the ventral periaqueductal grey; CN III fibres pass anteriorly through the red nucleus to exit in the interpeduncular fossa.
Red Nucleus: Prominent rounded nucleus in tegmentum (rich in iron/vascularity); gives rise to the rubrospinal tract (crosses in ventral tegmental decussation).
slides.remember: Superior colliculus = Vision/Eye reflexes + CN III (Oculomotor) + Red Nucleus + Substantia Nigra.
slides.q: Which nucleus at the superior colliculus level of the midbrain is the center for the pupillary light reflex?
slides.why: The pretectal nucleus receives retinal afferents via the optic tract and projects bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to mediate the pupillary light reflex.

slides.h: 2. White Matter Tracts in Crus Cerebri & Tegmentum
slides.p: Every viva examiner loves asking what runs in the crus cerebri and where the lemnisci sit at this upper midbrain level:
bullets: Crus Cerebri (medial to lateral): Medial 1/6 = Frontopontine fibres; Middle 2/3 = Pyramidal tracts (corticonuclear medially, corticospinal laterally); Lateral 1/6 = Temporopontine & Parietopontine fibres.

Sensory Lemnisci (in lateral tegmentum): From medial to lateral: Medial lemniscus, Trigeminothalamic tract, and Spinal lemniscus. (Note: Lateral lemniscus already ended in the inferior colliculus below!).
Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF): Lies just ventral to the oculomotor nucleus, coordinating conjugate eye movements.
slides.remember: Crus cerebri: 1/6 Frontopontine | 2/3 Pyramidal (Head medial, Leg lateral) | 1/6 Temporopontine. Lateral lemniscus is ABSENT here!
slides.q: Which lemniscus is NOT present in a transverse section of the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus?
slides.why: The lateral lemniscus (auditory pathway) terminates lower down in the inferior colliculus, so it is absent at the superior colliculus level.

slides.p: Occlusion of paramedian/peduncular branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) produces two classic midbrain syndromes at this level:
bullets: Weber's Syndrome (Ventral Midbrain): Damages crus cerebri + emerging CN III fibres → Ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, eye 'down & out', dilated fixed pupil) + Contralateral hemiplegia (including lower face).

Benedikt's Syndrome (Tegmentum): Damages red nucleus + medial lemniscus + CN III fibres → Ipsilateral CN III palsy + Contralateral involuntary movements (ataxia/tremor/chorea) + contralateral loss of proprioception/vibration.
slides.remember: Weber = Crus cerebri + CN III (Paralysis). Benedikt = Red nucleus + CN III (Tremor/Ataxia).
slides.q: A lesion involving the crus cerebri and emerging oculomotor nerve fibres at the superior colliculus level causes which syndrome?
slides.why: Weber's syndrome results from damage to the crus cerebri (causing contralateral hemiplegia) and exiting CN III fibres (causing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy).

lessons.title: Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)
quickRevision: 9th cranial nerve — mixed nerve of the 3rd pharyngeal arch (Motor, Parasympathetic, General Sensory, Taste, Visceral Sensory).

4 nuclei in medulla: Nucleus ambiguus (stylopharyngeus), Inferior salivatory nucleus (parotid), Nucleus of tractus solitarius (taste & carotid sinus/body), Spinal nucleus of trigeminal (general sensation).
Exits skull via Jugular Foramen (middle compartment) and passes between Internal & External Carotid Arteries.
Clinical: Loss of gag reflex (afferent limb) and Glossopharyngeal neuralgia.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Introduction & Functional Components (5 components) → 2. Deep Origin (4 nuclei in medulla) → 3. Superficial Attachment & Intracranial Course → 4. Exit through Jugular Foramen & Relations in Neck (superior & inferior ganglia) → 5. Branches & Distribution (Tympanic/Lesser petrosal, Carotid, Pharyngeal, Tonsillar, Lingual, Muscular) → 6. Applied Anatomy (Gag reflex, Glossopharyngeal neuralgia) + Diagram.

slides.p: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. Even though it is a slender nerve, it carries five distinct functional components arising from four nuclei in the medulla oblongata:
bullets: 1. Special Visceral Efferent (Branchial motor): From upper part of nucleus ambiguus → supplies only ONE muscle: stylopharyngeus.

2. General Visceral Efferent (Parasympathetic): From inferior salivatory nucleus → secretomotor to the parotid gland (via tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve).
3. Special Visceral Afferent (Taste): To nucleus of tractus solitarius (NTS) → carries taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue and circumvallate papillae.
4. General Visceral Afferent: To NTS → carries baroreceptor & chemoreceptor impulses from carotid sinus and carotid body.
5. General Somatic Afferent: To spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve → general sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue, palatine tonsil, pharynx, and middle ear.
slides.remember: CN IX supplies only ONE muscle (Stylopharyngeus) and ONE gland (Parotid), plus posterior 1/3 of tongue & carotid sinus/body!
slides.q: Which muscle is the ONLY skeletal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)?
slides.why: Stylopharyngeus is derived from the third pharyngeal arch and is the sole muscle innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

slides.p: CN IX emerges from the upper part of the postolivary sulcus of the medulla as 3–4 rootlets (above CN X and CN XI). It passes laterally across the flocculus of the cerebellum to exit the skull through the middle compartment of the jugular foramen.
bullets: Ganglia: Bears a small superior ganglion and a larger inferior (petrosal) ganglion in the jugular foramen.

Course in neck: Descends between the internal jugular vein and internal carotid artery, then curves forward around the posterior border of stylopharyngeus, passing between the internal and external carotid arteries.
Entry to pharynx: Passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle to reach the base of the tongue and tonsillar bed.
slides.remember: Exits Jugular Foramen → hugs Stylopharyngeus → passes BETWEEN Internal and External Carotid Arteries.
slides.q: Through which cranial foramen does the glossopharyngeal nerve exit the skull?
slides.why: CN IX exits through the middle compartment of the jugular foramen along with the inferior petrosal sinus, CN X, and CN XI.

slides.p: Memorize the six classic branches of CN IX and its clinical tests for your LAQ and viva:
bullets: 1. Tympanic nerve (of Jacobson): Enters middle ear → forms tympanic plexus → continues as lesser petrosal nerve to otic ganglion (parotid secretomotor).
2. Carotid branch (Nerve of Hering): Descends on ICA to carotid sinus (BP) and carotid body (O2/CO2).
3. Pharyngeal branches: Join vagus on middle constrictor to form pharyngeal plexus (sensory to pharynx).
4. Muscular branch: Supplies stylopharyngeus.
5. Tonsillar branches: Form circulus tonsillaris around palatine tonsil (referred ear pain in tonsillitis!).
6. Lingual branches: General sensation + taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue (including circumvallate papillae).

Clinical — Gag Reflex & Neuralgia: CN IX forms the afferent (sensory) limb of the gag reflex (CN X is efferent). Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes severe stabbing pain in the throat/tonsil radiating to the ear on swallowing.
slides.remember: Gag reflex: Afferent = CN IX (9), Efferent = CN X (10). Tonsillitis causes referred earache via tympanic branch of CN IX!
slides.q: In the pharyngeal gag reflex, which cranial nerve forms the afferent (sensory) limb?
slides.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries the sensory (afferent) impulse from the posterior pharyngeal wall/tonsillar pillar, while the vagus nerve (CN X) mediates the motor (efferent) pharyngeal contraction.

lessons.title: Oculomotor Nerve (CN III)
quickRevision: 3rd cranial nerve — purely motor (Somatic motor to 5 extraocular muscles + Parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae & ciliary muscle).
Arises from Oculomotor nuclear complex & Edinger-Westphal nucleus at superior colliculus level of midbrain.
Passes between PCA & SCA → lateral wall of Cavernous Sinus → divides into Superior & Inferior divisions → enters orbit via Superior Orbital Fissure (within tendinous ring).
Complete CN III palsy: Ptosis, Eye 'Down & Out', Dilated fixed pupil (mydriasis), Loss of accommodation.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Functional Components & Deep Origin (Oculomotor complex + Edinger-Westphal nucleus) → 2. Intracranial Course & Relations (PCA/SCA, Cavernous sinus lateral wall) → 3. Division & Entry into Orbit (Superior Orbital Fissure inside common tendinous ring) → 4. Distribution (Superior & Inferior divisions + Ciliary ganglion pathway) → 5. Applied Anatomy (Complete CN III palsy features & anatomical basis) + Diagram.

slides.p: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) is a purely motor cranial nerve with two components: General Somatic Efferent (GSE) for extraocular eye muscles, and General Visceral Efferent (GVE — parasympathetic) for intrinsic eye muscles.
bullets: Deep Origin: Somatic motor nucleus (in ventral periaqueductal grey at superior colliculus level) + Edinger-Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic).
Emergence: Emerges from the oculomotor sulcus on the medial side of the crus cerebri into the interpeduncular fossa.
Vascular Relation: Passes forward between the Posterior Cerebral Artery (above) and Superior Cerebellar Artery (below)—an important site for aneurysm compression!
Cavernous Sinus: Pierces dura to run forward in the upper part of the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (above CN IV).
slides.remember: CN III exits midbrain → sandwiched between PCA (top) & SCA (bottom) → lateral wall of Cavernous Sinus.
slides.q: The oculomotor nerve passes forward between which two arteries right after emerging from the midbrain?
opts: Anterior cerebral and middle cerebral arteries
Posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery
Anterior inferior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries
slides.why: CN III passes between the posterior cerebral artery (above) and the superior cerebellar artery (below) as it runs forward from the interpeduncular fossa.

slides.h: 2. Orbital Entry & Branches (Superior vs Inferior Division)
slides.p: Just before entering the orbit, CN III splits into a smaller superior division and a larger inferior division. Both divisions pass through the middle compartment of the superior orbital fissure, inside the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn), with the nasociliary nerve lying between them.
bullets: Superior Division supplies (2 muscles): Superior rectus and Levator palpebrae superioris.
Inferior Division supplies (3 extraocular muscles + parasympathetic): Medial rectus, Inferior rectus, and Inferior oblique.

Parasympathetic Pathway (Nerve to Inferior Oblique): Preganglionic fibres travel in the nerve to inferior oblique → synapse in the ciliary ganglion → postganglionic short ciliary nerves supply sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation).
slides.remember: All extraocular muscles are supplied by CN III EXCEPT SO4 (Superior Oblique = CN IV) and LR6 (Lateral Rectus = CN VI). Parasympathetic fibres hitchhike on the nerve to Inferior Oblique!
slides.q: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve reach the ciliary ganglion via which branch?
slides.why: The parasympathetic root of the ciliary ganglion leaves the nerve to the inferior oblique muscle (from the inferior division of CN III).

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Complete Oculomotor Nerve Palsy
slides.p: Every single clinical sign of a complete CN III lesion can be deduced directly from which muscles are paralyzed and which remain unopposed:
bullets: 1. Severe Ptosis (drooping of upper eyelid): Paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris.
2. Eyeball turned 'Down and Out': Unopposed action of Lateral Rectus (CN VI) pulls eye laterally ('out') and Superior Oblique (CN IV) pulls eye downward and laterally ('down').
3. Dilated, Fixed Pupil (Mydriasis): Paralysis of sphincter pupillae leaves dilator pupillae (sympathetic) unopposed; both direct and consensual light reflexes are lost on that side.
4. Loss of Accommodation: Paralysis of ciliary muscle causes blurred near vision.
5. Diplopia (Double Vision): Present once the drooping eyelid is lifted.
slides.remember: Complete CN III palsy = Ptosis + Eye 'Down & Out' (SO4 & LR6 win!) + Dilated fixed pupil + Loss of accommodation.
slides.q: Why does the eyeball point 'down and out' in complete oculomotor nerve (CN III) paralysis?
opts: Overactivity of superior rectus and medial rectus
Unopposed action of lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV)
Spasm of the inferior oblique muscle
slides.why: With CN III paralyzed, the only functioning extraocular muscles are the lateral rectus (abducts the eye 'out') and superior oblique (depresses and abducts the eye 'down').

lessons.title: Functional Areas in Frontal Lobe
quickRevision: Primary Motor Area (Area 4): Precentral gyrus; contralateral motor homunculus (head/hand huge, leg on paracentral lobule).
Premotor (Area 6) & Supplementary Motor Area (SMA): Planning and programming of skilled movements.
Frontal Eye Field (Area 8): Conjugate horizontal eye movements to the opposite side.
Broca's Motor Speech Area (Areas 44 & 45): Pars opercularis & pars triangularis of inferior frontal gyrus (dominant/left hemisphere) → lesion causes expressive/motor aphasia.
Prefrontal Cortex (Areas 9–12): Personality, judgment, executive planning, social behavior.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Introduction & Boundaries of Frontal Lobe (Central sulcus, Lateral sulcus) → 2. Sulci & Gyri of Frontal Lobe (briefly) → 3. Detailed Functional Areas with Brodmann Numbers (Area 4, Area 6 & SMA, Area 8, Areas 44 & 45 Broca's, Prefrontal Cortex) → 4. Blood Supply (ACA on medial/paracentral, MCA on superolateral) → 5. Applied Anatomy (Motor aphasia, Frontal lobe syndrome, Gaze palsy) + Superolateral & Medial hemisphere diagrams.

slides.p: The frontal lobe lies in front of the central sulcus (of Rolando) and above the lateral sulcus (of Sylvius). Its primary motor cortex—Brodmann Area 4—occupies the precentral gyrus and the anterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial surface.
bullets: Function: Initiates voluntary skilled movements of the opposite (contralateral) half of the body via the corticospinal and corticonuclear tracts (contains giant pyramidal Betz cells).

Motor Homunculus (Upside-Down Representation): From inferior to superior along the precentral gyrus: Pharynx/Tongue → Face → Hand/Fingers → Trunk; and continuing onto the medial paracentral lobule: Leg → Foot → Perineum.
Cortical Magnification: Areas performing fine movements (lips, tongue, thumb, fingers) have disproportionately huge cortical representation.
slides.remember: Area 4 = Precentral gyrus. Face & Hand sit on lateral surface (MCA supply); Leg & Foot sit on medial paracentral lobule (ACA supply).
slides.q: Which part of the body is represented on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule?
slides.why: The motor and sensory representations of the lower limb and perineum extend over the superomedial border onto the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

slides.h: 2. Premotor (Area 6), Frontal Eye Field (Area 8) & Broca's Area (44, 45)
slides.p: Anterior to the primary motor cortex lie specialized association motor areas that plan movements, steer the eyes, and produce speech:
bullets: Premotor Cortex (Area 6) & Supplementary Motor Area (SMA): Lies in front of Area 4; stores motor programs and coordinates complex learned movements (e.g., playing guitar or writing).
Frontal Eye Field (Area 8): Located in the posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus; controls voluntary conjugate deviation of both eyes to the opposite side.

Broca's Motor Speech Area (Areas 44 & 45): Located in the pars opercularis (44) and pars triangularis (45) of the inferior frontal gyrus, usually in the left (dominant) hemisphere. Coordinates muscles of larynx, pharynx, tongue, and lips for fluent speech.
slides.remember: Area 4 = Moves muscles. Area 6 = Plans movement. Area 8 = Moves eyes to opposite side. Areas 44, 45 = Broca's spoken words!
slides.q: Broca's motor speech area corresponds to which Brodmann areas in the inferior frontal gyrus?
slides.why: Broca's area occupies Brodmann areas 44 (pars opercularis) and 45 (pars triangularis) of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.

slides.p: The anterior pole of the frontal lobe (Areas 9, 10, 11, 12) is the prefrontal cortex—the seat of human personality, foresight, judgment, emotional regulation, and social appropriateness. Let's review the clinical syndromes of frontal lobe lesions:
bullets: Broca's (Expressive / Motor) Aphasia: Lesion of Areas 44 & 45 in dominant hemisphere → patient understands spoken and written language well, but speaks slowly with great effort, poor grammar, and telegraphic phrases.
Frontal Eye Field (Area 8) Lesion: Irritative lesion turns eyes to the opposite side; destructive stroke causes eyes to look toward the side of the lesion ('eyes look at the lesion').
Prefrontal Lobe Syndrome: Loss of social inhibition, apathy, poor judgment, personality changes, and reappearance of primitive reflexes (grasp/suck reflex).
slides.remember: Broca's aphasia = Comprehension intact, speech broken ('broken words'). Area 8 stroke = 'Eyes look toward the healthy hemisphere? No—eyes look AT the lesion!'
slides.q: A patient understands questions completely but speaks in slow, effortful, telegraphic phrases after a left inferior frontal gyrus stroke. Which area is damaged?
slides.why: Damage to Broca's area (Areas 44 and 45) produces expressive (motor) aphasia, characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.

lessons.title: Superolateral Surface of Cerebrum
quickRevision: 3 poles (Frontal, Occipital, Temporal) and 3 borders (Superomedial, Inferolateral, Medial orbital/occipital).

3 main sulci divide the surface into 4 lobes: Central sulcus (of Rolando), Lateral sulcus (of Sylvius — stem + anterior horizontal, anterior ascending, posterior rami), and Parieto-occipital sulcus (cuts superomedial border ~5 cm in front of occipital pole).
Frontal lobe: Precentral gyrus (Area 4), Superior/Middle/Inferior frontal gyri (Broca's area 44, 45 in inferior frontal gyrus).
Parietal lobe: Postcentral gyrus (Areas 3, 1, 2 — primary sensory), Superior & Inferior parietal lobules (Supramarginal & Angular gyri).
Temporal lobe: Superior/Middle/Inferior temporal gyri; Heschl's gyrus (Areas 41, 42 — primary auditory) & Wernicke's area (Area 22 — sensory speech).

Blood supply: Almost the entire superolateral surface is supplied by the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA), EXCEPT a 1-inch strip along superomedial border (ACA) and occipital pole/lower temporal border (PCA).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Poles & Borders → 2. Main Sulci Dividing Lobes (Central, Lateral with its 3 rami, Parieto-occipital + Pre-occipital notch imaginary lines) → 3. Sulci & Gyri of Each Lobe (Frontal, Parietal, Temporal, Occipital + Insula) → 4. Key Functional Areas (Motor, Sensory, Broca's, Wernicke's, Auditory, Visual) → 5. Arterial Supply (MCA territory + ACA/PCA strips) → 6. Applied Anatomy (MCA stroke, Aphasias) + Large labelled diagram of superolateral surface.

slides.p: The superolateral surface of each cerebral hemisphere is convex and lies beneath the cranial vault. It has three poles (frontal, occipital, temporal) and is divided into four major lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) by three key sulci and two imaginary lines:
bullets: Central Sulcus (of Rolando): Starts at the superomedial border slightly behind the midpoint between frontal and occipital poles, and runs downward and forward toward the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus (stops just short of it).

Lateral Sulcus (of Sylvius): Deep cleft on the inferior/lateral aspect; its stem divides at the Sylvian point into anterior horizontal, anterior ascending, and posterior rami. Deep inside its floor lies the hidden 5th lobe: the Insula.

Parieto-occipital Sulcus & Pre-occipital Notch: Parieto-occipital sulcus cuts the superomedial border ~5 cm in front of the occipital pole. An imaginary line from it to the pre-occipital notch separates the occipital lobe, and a second line from the posterior ramus of lateral sulcus to the first line separates parietal from temporal lobes.
slides.remember: Lateral sulcus has 3 rami: Anterior Horizontal, Anterior Ascending, and Posterior. Hidden inside = Insula!
slides.q: Which lobe of the cerebral hemisphere lies hidden deep in the floor of the lateral sulcus?
slides.why: The insula is submerged deep within the lateral sulcus and is covered by opercula of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes.

slides.h: 2. Sulci, Gyri & Functional Areas of Each Lobe
slides.p: Organize the sulci and gyri lobe-by-lobe so you can draw and label them cleanly in your LAQ:
bullets: Frontal Lobe: Precentral sulcus outlines the precentral gyrus (Primary Motor Area 4). Superior & inferior frontal sulci divide the rest into superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri. The anterior horizontal and ascending rami of lateral sulcus divide the inferior frontal gyrus into pars orbitalis, pars triangularis (Area 45), and pars opercularis (Area 44) = Broca's motor speech area.

Parietal Lobe: Postcentral sulcus outlines the postcentral gyrus (Primary Somatosensory Areas 3, 1, 2). Intraparietal sulcus divides the rest into superior and inferior parietal lobules (containing supramarginal gyrus around posterior ramus and angular gyrus around superior temporal sulcus).

Temporal Lobe: Superior & inferior temporal sulci create superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri. Upper surface of superior temporal gyrus bears transverse temporal gyri of Heschl (Primary Auditory Areas 41, 42); posterior part is Wernicke's sensory speech area (Area 22).
Occipital Lobe: Lateral occipital sulcus and lunate sulcus; receives extensions of primary and association visual cortex (Areas 17, 18, 19) near the occipital pole.
slides.remember: Precentral gyrus = Motor (4). Postcentral gyrus = Sensory (3, 1, 2). Inferior frontal = Broca (44, 45). Superior temporal = Auditory (41, 42) + Wernicke (22).
slides.q: Where is Wernicke's sensory speech area (Area 22) located?
opts: Posterior part of superior temporal gyrus
slides.why: Wernicke's area (Brodmann area 22) is situated in the posterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

slides.p: Blood supply of the superolateral surface is a favorite viva and MCQ question:
bullets: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA): Supplies most of the superolateral surface (including face & upper limb motor/sensory areas, Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and auditory cortex).
Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA): Supplies a narrow 1-inch (2.5 cm) strip along the superomedial border down to the parieto-occipital sulcus (lower limb motor/sensory strip).
Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA): Supplies the occipital pole / visual cortex and the inferior temporal gyrus along the inferolateral border.

Clinical — MCA Occlusion: Causes contralateral paralysis and sensory loss predominantly affecting the face and upper limb (sparing the lower limb), plus aphasia if the dominant (left) hemisphere is affected.
slides.remember: MCA = Main superolateral surface (Face + Arm + Speech). ACA = Top 1-inch strip (Leg). PCA = Back tip (Occipital/Vision).
slides.q: Which artery supplies the narrow 1-inch strip along the superomedial border on the superolateral surface of the cerebrum?
slides.why: Branches of the anterior cerebral artery curve over the superomedial border to supply a 1-inch strip of cortex on the superolateral surface.

lessons.title: Pons
quickRevision: Middle part of brainstem (~2.5 cm long) between midbrain above and medulla below; connected to cerebellum by Middle Cerebellar Peduncles.
External features: Ventral surface has midline Basilar Sulcus (basilar artery) and CN V attachment laterally; Pontomedullary junction gives attachment to CN VI, VII, VIII (medial to lateral).

Internal division by Trapezoid Body into: 1. Ventral (Basilar) part (pontine nuclei, corticospinal/corticonuclear tracts, transverse pontocerebellar fibres) and 2. Dorsal (Tegmental) part (cranial nerve nuclei V, VI, VII, VIII + lemnisci + MLF).
Clinical: Millard-Gubler syndrome (CN VI + CN VII + corticospinal tract) and Pontine hemorrhage (pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, coma).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Situation & Dimensions → 2. External Features (Anterior/Ventral surface, Posterior/Dorsal surface forming upper floor of 4th ventricle, Cranial nerve attachments) → 3. Internal Structure (Basilar part vs Tegmental part at Lower Pons [Facial colliculus level] & Upper Pons [Trigeminal level]) → 4. Blood Supply (Pontine branches of Basilar artery) → 5. Applied Anatomy (Millard-Gubler syndrome, Pontine hemorrhage) + Two labelled T.S. diagrams.

slides.p: The pons ('bridge') is the middle segment of the brainstem (~2.5 cm long), lying on the clivus between the midbrain above and the medulla oblongata below. Its prominent transverse fibres bundle together on each side as the middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis), linking the cerebrum to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere.
bullets: Anterior (Ventral) Surface: Convex from side to side; shows a vertical midline groove—the basilar sulcus—lodging the basilar artery. Lateral to this, the large trigeminal nerve (CN V) emerges (large sensory root + small motor root).

Pontomedullary Sulcus (Inferior Border): Three cranial nerves emerge from medial to lateral: Abducens (CN VI) above pyramid, Facial (CN VII), and Vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) at the cerebellopontine angle.
Posterior (Dorsal) Surface: Hidden by the cerebellum; forms the upper triangular half of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
slides.remember: Pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral): 6, 7, 8 (CN VI, VII, VIII). Mid-pons laterally: 5 (CN V).
slides.q: Which cranial nerves emerge from medial to lateral at the pontomedullary junction?
slides.why: At the inferior border of the pons (pontomedullary groove), CN VI, CN VII, and CN VIII emerge in order from medial to lateral.

slides.h: 2. Internal Structure: Basilar Part vs Tegmentum
slides.p: A transverse section of the pons is divided by the transverse auditory fibres of the trapezoid body into an anterior basilar (ventral) part and a posterior tegmental (dorsal) part:
bullets: Basilar (Ventral) Part (same at all levels): Contains scattered pontine nuclei (relaying corticopontine impulses), vertical bundles of corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres, and transverse pontocerebellar fibres that cross the midline to enter the opposite middle cerebellar peduncle.

Tegmentum — Lower Pons (Facial Colliculus Level): Contains abducens nucleus (CN VI), facial motor nucleus (CN VII) whose fibres loop around CN VI to form the facial colliculus, spinal nucleus of CN V, vestibular & cochlear nuclei, MLF, and the 4 lemnisci (Medial, Trigeminal, Spinal, Lateral from medial to lateral).
Tegmentum — Upper Pons (Trigeminal Level): Contains the motor nucleus and principal (chief) sensory nucleus of CN V, plus the superior cerebellar peduncles.
slides.remember: Ventral pons = Motor highway + Pontocerebellar bridge. Dorsal tegmentum = Nuclei of CN V, VI, VII, VIII + Trapezoid body + 4 Lemnisci.
slides.q: Which structure divides the pons internally into a ventral basilar part and a dorsal tegmental part?
slides.why: The trapezoid body (decussating auditory fibres) lies at the boundary between the ventral basilar pons and the dorsal pontine tegmentum.

slides.p: The pons is supplied by paramedian and circumferential pontine branches of the basilar artery. Vascular lesions produce very distinct clinical presentations:
bullets: Millard-Gubler Syndrome (Ventral Caudal Pons): Damages emerging CN VI + CN VII + corticospinal tract → Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (medial squint), ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis, and contralateral hemiplegia.

Pontine Hemorrhage: Bilateral destruction of descending sympathetic fibres + reticular activating system causes classic pinpoint pupils (unopposed parasympathetic tone), hyperpyrexia (high fever), quadriplegia, and deep coma.
Locked-in Syndrome: Ventral pontine infarction spares consciousness and vertical eye movements/blinking, but paralyzes all four limbs and speech.
slides.remember: Pontine hemorrhage triad = Pinpoint pupils + Hyperpyrexia + Deep coma. Millard-Gubler = CN 6 + CN 7 + Opposite body weak.
slides.q: A massive pontine hemorrhage classically produces which characteristic pupillary sign?
slides.why: Pontine hemorrhage interrupts descending sympathetic pupillodilator fibres bilaterally while sparing the midbrain Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nuclei, causing pinpoint pupils.

lessons.title: Midbrain (Mesencephalon)
quickRevision: Shortest, uppermost part of brainstem (~2 cm) connecting pons/cerebellum below to forebrain above; traversed by Cerebral Aqueduct (of Sylvius).

External features: Ventrally = Cerebral peduncles + Interpeduncular fossa (CN III exit); Dorsally = Tectum with 4 colliculi (Corpora quadrigemina) + CN IV exit below inferior colliculus (only CN exiting dorsally!).
Lower Midbrain (Inferior Colliculus level): Inferior colliculus (auditory), Trochlear nucleus (CN IV), Decussation of Superior Cerebellar Peduncles, all 4 lemnisci.
Upper Midbrain (Superior Colliculus level): Superior colliculus (visual reflexes), Pretectal nucleus, Oculomotor complex (CN III + Edinger-Westphal), Red nucleus, Rubrospinal decussation.
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Situation & Dimensions → 2. External Features (Ventral: crus cerebri & interpeduncular fossa; Dorsal: tectum, superior & inferior colliculi, brachia, CN IV exit) → 3. Internal Subdivisions (Tectum, Tegmentum, Substantia Nigra, Crus Cerebri) → 4. T.S. at Inferior Colliculus Level → 5. T.S. at Superior Colliculus Level → 6. Blood Supply & Clinical Syndromes (Weber's, Benedikt's, Parinaud's) + Both T.S. diagrams.

slides.p: The midbrain (mesencephalon) is the shortest segment of the brainstem (~2 cm long), passing through the tentorial notch to connect the hindbrain with the diencephalon. It is traversed by the narrow cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) connecting the 3rd and 4th ventricles.
bullets: Dorsal Surface (Tectum): Shows four rounded swellings—the corpora quadrigemina: two superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (auditory relay). Immediately below the inferior colliculus emerges the trochlear nerve (CN IV)—the ONLY cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem!
Ventral Surface: Presents two massive diverging fibre bundles—the crus cerebri—separated by the interpeduncular fossa, from whose medial sulcus emerges the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
Internal Zones: Tectum (behind aqueduct) + Cerebral peduncles (in front), each divided by the pigmented substantia nigra into posterior tegmentum and anterior crus cerebri.
slides.remember: Superior colliculus = Sight (visual). Inferior colliculus = Sound (auditory). CN IV exits dorsally below inferior colliculus!
slides.q: Which cranial nerve is the ONLY one to emerge from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem?
slides.why: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) decussates inside the superior medullary velum and emerges on the dorsal surface of the midbrain just below the inferior colliculus.

slides.h: 2. Transverse Sections: Inferior vs Superior Colliculus Levels
slides.p: In an LAQ on Midbrain, comparing the two classic transverse section levels earns full marks:
bullets: Level 1 — Inferior Colliculus (Lower Midbrain): Contains Inferior colliculus (auditory), Trochlear nucleus (CN IV) in ventral periaqueductal grey, Mesencephalic nucleus of CN V (proprioception from face/muscles of mastication), Decussation of Superior Cerebellar Peduncles in central tegmentum, and all 4 lemnisci (Medial, Trigeminal, Spinal, Lateral).

Level 2 — Superior Colliculus (Upper Midbrain): Contains Superior colliculus, Pretectal nucleus (light reflex), Oculomotor nucleus (CN III) + Edinger-Westphal nucleus, prominent Red nucleus, ventral & dorsal tegmental decussations, and 3 lemnisci (Lateral lemniscus has already ended below).
Substantia Nigra (Both Levels): Dark melanin-rich dopaminergic neurons projecting to striatum; degeneration causes Parkinson's disease.
slides.remember: Lower Midbrain = CN IV + Superior Cerebellar Peduncle Decussation + 4 Lemnisci. Upper Midbrain = CN III + Red Nucleus + 3 Lemnisci.
slides.q: Which prominent decussation occupies the central tegmentum of the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus?
slides.why: Fibres of the superior cerebellar peduncles cross the midline in the central tegmentum at the inferior colliculus level on their way to the red nucleus and thalamus.

slides.p: The midbrain is supplied chiefly by branches of the Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) and Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA):
bullets: Parinaud's Syndrome (Dorsal Midbrain): Compression of the superior colliculi/pretectal area (e.g., by a pineal gland tumor) causes paralysis of upward gaze and loss of pupillary light reflex with preserved accommodation (light-near dissociation).
Weber's Syndrome: Ventral midbrain lesion (crus cerebri + CN III) → ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiplegia.
Benedikt's Syndrome: Tegmental lesion (red nucleus + medial lemniscus + CN III) → ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral tremor/ataxia + loss of proprioception.
slides.remember: Pineal tumor presses Superior Colliculus → Parinaud's syndrome (cannot look UP!).
slides.q: Compression of the dorsal midbrain (superior colliculus area) by a pineal tumor characteristically impairs which eye movement?
slides.why: Lesions of the superior colliculus and pretectal region (Parinaud's syndrome) classically cause paralysis of conjugate upward gaze.

lessons.title: T.S. Medulla Oblongata – Pyramidal Decussation
quickRevision: Lowest level of closed medulla oblongata (motor decussation level), closely resembling the cervical spinal cord.

75–90% of corticospinal (pyramidal) fibres cross the midline in the anterior median fissure as bundles, severing the anterior grey horn from central grey matter to form the Lateral Corticospinal Tract.
Remaining 10–25% uncrossed fibres continue down as the Anterior Corticospinal Tract.
Posteriorly: Fasciculus gracilis & fasciculus cuneatus with the lower ends of nucleus gracilis & nucleus cuneatus; laterally: Spinal nucleus & tract of trigeminal nerve (CN V).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Level & General Appearance (closed medulla, central canal present) → 2. Great Motor (Pyramidal) Decussation (75–90% crossing to lateral corticospinal tract, detachment of anterior grey horn) → 3. Grey Matter Features (central grey matter, nucleus gracilis/cuneatus, spinal nucleus of CN V, detached anterior horn = supraspinal/spinal accessory nucleus) → 4. White Matter Tracts (dorsal columns, spinocerebellar, spinothalamic) → 5. Neat labelled transverse section diagram.

slides.p: A transverse section through the lower part of the closed medulla oblongata passes through the pyramidal (motor) decussation. At first glance it looks almost like the upper cervical spinal cord, with a small central canal surrounded by central grey matter—except for one dramatic feature in front:
bullets: Pyramidal Decussation: In the anterior pyramids, 75% to 90% of corticospinal fibres sweep backward and across the midline in interdigitating bundles, obliterating the anterior median fissure.
Formation of Lateral Corticospinal Tract: After crossing, these fibres descend in the lateral white column of the spinal cord as the lateral corticospinal tract.
Anterior Corticospinal Tract: The remaining 10% to 25% of uncrossed fibres continue straight down near the anterior median fissure as the anterior corticospinal tract.
slides.remember: 75–90% cross here → Lateral Corticospinal Tract. 10–25% stay uncrossed → Anterior Corticospinal Tract.
slides.q: Approximately what percentage of corticospinal fibres cross the midline at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla?
slides.why: About 75–90% of corticospinal fibres decussate in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract, while the remaining 10–25% descend ipsilaterally in the anterior corticospinal tract.

slides.h: 2. Grey Matter Changes Caused by the Crossing Fibres
slides.p: As the thick bundles of crossing pyramidal fibres slice backward and laterally, they physically cut through the anterior grey column:
bullets: Detached Anterior Grey Horn: Separated from the central grey matter; its medial part becomes the supraspinal nucleus (for C1) and its lateral part becomes the spinal nucleus of the accessory nerve (CN XI).
Nucleus Gracilis & Nucleus Cuneatus: Appear as slender projections extending backward from the central grey matter into the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.
Spinal Nucleus & Tract of Trigeminal Nerve (CN V): Lie on the posterolateral aspect (continuous below with the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord).
slides.remember: Crossing pyramid fibres slice off the anterior grey horn → forms Spinal Accessory (CN XI) & Supraspinal nuclei!
slides.q: Which nucleus in the posterolateral closed medulla is directly continuous below with the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord?
opts: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve (CN V)
slides.why: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (carrying pain and temperature from the face) continues inferiorly into the substantia gelatinosa of the cervical spinal cord.

slides.p: Around the periphery of the section sit the ascending sensory tracts travelling up from the spinal cord, plus a classic clinical lesion pattern:
bullets: Posteriorly: Fasciculus gracilis (medial, lower limb) and fasciculus cuneatus (lateral, upper limb).
Laterally: Posterior spinocerebellar tract, anterior spinocerebellar tract, and lateral spinothalamic tract (spinal lemniscus).

Clinical — Cruciate Hemiplegia: Because arm fibres cross slightly higher in the pyramidal decussation than leg fibres, a selective midline lesion at the decussation can injure crossed arm fibres and uncrossed leg fibres, causing paralysis of one arm and the opposite leg (cruciate paralysis).
slides.remember: Cruciate paralysis = lesion right at the pyramidal decussation → one arm + opposite leg paralyzed!
slides.q: A selective lesion at the pyramidal decussation affecting crossed upper-limb fibres and uncrossed lower-limb fibres causes:
opts: Cruciate hemiplegia (one arm and opposite leg)
Pure sensory loss of the face
slides.why: Because upper-limb corticospinal fibres decussate superiorly to lower-limb fibres, a localized lesion here can produce cruciate paralysis affecting one upper limb and the contralateral lower limb.

lessons.title: Inferior Cerebellar Peduncle (Restiform Body)
quickRevision: Thick rope-like white matter bundle (Restiform body) on the posterolateral aspect of the upper medulla connecting medulla & spinal cord to the cerebellum.
Carries predominantly AFFERENT (incoming) tracts to cerebellum (unlike Superior Cerebellar Peduncle which is mainly efferent).

Major Afferents (5): Posterior spinocerebellar tract, Olivocerebellar tract (climbing fibres from opposite inferior olivary nucleus), Cuneocerebellar tract (posterior external arcuate fibres), Parolivocerebellar, Reticulocerebellar & Vestibulocerebellar fibres (via juxtarestiform body).
Major Efferents (2): Cerebellovestibular and Cerebelloreticular fibres (running in the medial Juxtarestiform body).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Definition & Location (restiform body, inferolateral boundary of 4th ventricle) → 2. Two Functional Parts (Restiform body vs Juxtarestiform body) → 3. Afferent Fibres Entering Cerebellum (list all 5–6 with origins!) → 4. Efferent Fibres Leaving Cerebellum → 5. Applied Anatomy (Lateral medullary / PICA syndrome lesion → ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia) + Schematic diagram.

slides.h: 1. What is it, Location & Two Parts?
slides.p: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (also called the restiform body) is a thick, rope-like bundle of nerve fibres located on the posterolateral aspect of the upper (open) medulla oblongata. It forms the inferolateral boundary of the fourth ventricle and curves upward into the cerebellum.
bullets: 1. Restiform Body (Main Lateral Part): Purely afferent—carries sensory and motor-planning signals from the spinal cord and medulla INTO the cerebellum.
2. Juxtarestiform Body (Small Medial Part): Lies close to the vestibular nuclei and carries two-way (afferent & efferent) vestibulocerebellar fibres.
Key Contrast with Other Peduncles: Inferior & Middle peduncles are mainly afferent to the cerebellum, whereas the Superior cerebellar peduncle is mainly efferent.
slides.remember: Inferior & Middle peduncles bring info IN to cerebellum; Superior peduncle sends commands OUT!
slides.q: Which part of the inferior cerebellar peduncle carries reciprocal connections between the vestibular nuclei and the cerebellum?
slides.why: The medial juxtarestiform body carries both afferent vestibulocerebellar and efferent cerebellovestibular fibres.

slides.p: Memorizing the exact list of tracts passing through the inferior cerebellar peduncle is the heart of this starred Short Note:
bullets: 1. Posterior Spinocerebellar Tract: Uncrossed unconscious proprioception from lower limb & trunk (Clarke's column) → ipsilateral cerebellum.
2. Cuneocerebellar Tract (Posterior External Arcuate Fibres): Uncrossed proprioception from upper limb & neck (accessory cuneate nucleus).
3. Olivocerebellar Tract: Largest component! Arises from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus, crosses the midline, and ends as climbing fibres in cerebellar cortex.
4. Reticulocerebellar & Arcuatocerebellar Fibres: From medullary reticular formation and arcuate nuclei (via striae medullares).
5. Vestibulocerebellar Fibres (Juxtarestiform): From vestibular nerve and vestibular nuclei to flocculonodular lobe.
Efferent Fibres (Juxtarestiform): Cerebellovestibular and cerebelloreticular fibres projecting out from fastigial nucleus/flocculonodular lobe.
slides.remember: Remember 'P-O-C-R-V' entering: Posterior spinocerebellar, Olivocerebellar (climbing fibres!), Cuneocerebellar, Reticulocerebellar, Vestibulocerebellar.
slides.q: Which tract passing through the inferior cerebellar peduncle originates from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus and terminates as climbing fibres?
slides.why: Olivocerebellar fibres arise from the opposite inferior olivary nucleus, cross the midline, enter the inferior cerebellar peduncle, and terminate as climbing fibres on Purkinje cells.

slides.p: How does a lesion of the inferior cerebellar peduncle show up clinically?
bullets: Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome: Occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) damages the inferior cerebellar peduncle along with spinocerebellar tracts.

Result — Ipsilateral Cerebellar Ataxia: Because cerebellar connections are predominantly ipsilateral, damage to the right inferior cerebellar peduncle causes clumsiness, loss of balance, dysmetria (past-pointing), and intention tremor on the SAME (right) side.
slides.remember: Cerebellar signs are ALWAYS IPSILATERAL (same side as lesion)! PICA stroke damages Inferior Cerebellar Peduncle → same-side ataxia.
slides.q: Damage to the right inferior cerebellar peduncle (as in PICA thrombosis) produces cerebellar ataxia on which side of the body?
slides.why: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls coordination on the same side of the body, so damage to the right inferior cerebellar peduncle causes ipsilateral (right-sided) ataxia.

lessons.title: T.S. Spinal Cord – Cervical Level
quickRevision: Large oval cross-section (cervical enlargement C5–T1 for brachial plexus) with abundant white matter (contains tracts for ALL body levels).
H-shaped central grey matter: Large, broad anterior grey horn (numerous motor neurons for upper limb muscles) and slender posterior grey horn; NO lateral horn in lower cervical segments.
Posterior funiculus is clearly divided by the posterior intermediate septum into medial Fasciculus Gracilis (leg) and lateral Fasciculus Cuneatus (arm).

Major tracts: Ascending (Fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus, Lateral & Anterior spinothalamic, Posterior & Anterior spinocerebellar) + Descending (Lateral & Anterior corticospinal, Rubrospinal, Vestibulospinal).
lessons.examFramework: Write under: 1. Distinguishing Features of Cervical Level (large oval shape, huge white matter, broad anterior horn, presence of BOTH fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus, absence of lateral horn) → 2. Grey Matter Organization (Anterior horn nuclei, Posterior horn laminae/substantia gelatinosa) → 3. White Matter Funiculi & Tracts (Posterior, Lateral, Anterior columns — list ascending & descending tracts) → 4. Blood Supply (1 Anterior + 2 Posterior spinal arteries) + Large labelled T.S. diagram.

slides.h: 1. How to Identify Cervical Level Immediately (Histology & Gross)
slides.p: In both theory exams and histology/neuroanatomy spotting, examiners love asking how you recognize a transverse section of the cervical spinal cord:
bullets: 1. Large & Oval Shape: Horizontally oval (transverse diameter > anteroposterior diameter), especially large at C5–T1 due to the cervical enlargement supplying the upper limbs.
2. Abundant White Matter: Has the largest amount of white matter of any spinal level because ALL ascending tracts from below and ALL descending tracts from the brain pass through it.
3. Broad Anterior Grey Horn: Thick and well-developed (housing medial & lateral motor neuron groups for neck and upper limb muscles).

4. Posterior Funiculus Split in Two: Shows BOTH fasciculus gracilis (medially) and fasciculus cuneatus (laterally) separated by a posterior intermediate septum. (Below T6, fasciculus cuneatus is absent!)
5. No Lateral Grey Horn: Lateral horn is a feature of T1–L2 (sympathetic), not cervical segments.
slides.remember: Cervical T.S. spotting clues = Oval + Huge white matter + Fat anterior horn + BOTH Gracilis & Cuneatus + NO lateral horn!
slides.q: Which ascending tract in the posterior white column is present in cervical and upper thoracic segments (above T6) but ABSENT in lumbar segments?
slides.why: Fasciculus cuneatus carries proprioception and fine touch from the upper limb and upper thorax (above T6), so it is present in cervical sections but absent in lower thoracic and lumbar sections.

slides.h: 2. Grey Matter Nuclei & White Matter Tracts
slides.p: Organize the internal structures neatly into Grey Matter and the Three White Funiculi:
bullets: Grey Matter: Anterior horn contains medial group (neck/axial muscles) and lateral group (upper limb muscles; plus phrenic nucleus in C3–C5). Posterior horn contains substantia gelatinosa (pain gate), nucleus proprius, and marginal zone.
Posterior Funiculus (Ascending): Fasciculus gracilis (medial) & Fasciculus cuneatus (lateral) — conscious proprioception, vibration, and two-point discrimination.

Lateral Funiculus: Ascending = Posterior & anterior spinocerebellar tracts (peripherally), Lateral spinothalamic tract (pain & temperature). Descending = Lateral corticospinal tract (medial to posterior spinocerebellar), rubrospinal tract.

Anterior Funiculus: Ascending = Anterior spinothalamic tract (crude touch & pressure). Descending = Anterior corticospinal tract (next to anterior median fissure), vestibulospinal & tectospinal tracts.
slides.remember: Posterior column = Conscious proprioception/vibration. Lateral column = Lateral corticospinal (motor) + Lateral spinothalamic (pain/temp) + Spinocerebellar.
slides.q: Where is the lateral corticospinal tract located in a transverse section of the cervical spinal cord?
opts: In the posterior funiculus medial to fasciculus gracilis
In the lateral funiculus, medial to the posterior spinocerebellar tract
Adjacent to the anterior median fissure
slides.why: The lateral corticospinal tract descends in the posterior part of the lateral funiculus, just medial to the posterior spinocerebellar tract and lateral to the posterior grey horn.

slides.p: Wrap up your short note with arterial supply and two high-yield cervical cord clinical correlations:
bullets: Arterial Supply: Single Anterior Spinal Artery (in anterior median fissure; supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including corticospinal & spinothalamic tracts) + paired Posterior Spinal Arteries (supply posterior 1/3 including dorsal columns).

Syringomyelia (Cervical Cord): Central canal cavitation damages decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure → bilateral dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain & temperature in a 'cape-like' distribution across shoulders and arms, with preserved touch/vibration).
High Cervical Injury (Above C3): Interrupts descending pathways to the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) → diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory arrest ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive').
slides.remember: C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive! Cervical syringomyelia = 'Cape-like' loss of pain & temperature with preserved touch.
slides.q: Cystic cavitation around the central canal in the cervical spinal cord (syringomyelia) characteristically causes bilateral loss of:
opts: Pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution across shoulders and upper limbs
Voluntary movement of the lower limbs only
slides.why: Syringomyelia interrupts pain and temperature fibres decussating in the anterior white commissure at cervical segments, producing bilateral dissociated anesthesia over the shoulders and upper limbs.
